text.p: An initiative launched by the securities commissions in Latvia and Estonia to lay the groundwork for an eventual merger of Baltic stock markets has been welcomed by dealers and analysts.
Dealers say that one regional exchange would attract more foreign investment than the three small bourses combined and strengthen the partners' comptetitveness against other emerging markets.
But talks are only in their infant stage and a blue-print for a pan-Baltic market remains a long way off.
"There is no doubt about the need for us (Baltic bourses) to merge into a single market as soon as possible," Viktors Gustons, the chairman of the Latvian securities commission, said last week.
"In principle, we support the idea of merging, but it is too early to say what form a merger would take," Helo Meigas, the managing director of the Tallinn stock exchange, told Reuters.
"At this moment, we are interested in harmonising requirements and exchanging real time trading information and company announcements," she said.

If a single market is created, the Balts would be following a trail blazed by Nordic neighbours Sweden and Denmark, which plan to introduce a joint share-trading system between the summer of 1998 and 1999.
Latvian officials have said that a combined Baltic exchange might eventually attach itself to a larger market in the neighbourhood, probably in Scandinavia.
Estonia and Latvia have taken the first tentative step towards cooperation with an agreement which allows security transations from each country to be kept in accounts in the others' depository.
That agreement comes into effect Tuesday.
Lithuania's bourse and securities commission have not yet committed themselves to the depository agreement and seem less enthusiastic about the notion of merger than their Baltic counterparts.
But Lithuanian dealers are bullish on the idea of a single regional market.
"The markets should eventually be combined," said Tomas Andrejauskas, of Lithuania's Suprema Brokerage firm.
"Right now, each individual market is too small to attract the interest of big overseas investors...and foreign investors tend to view the "Baltics" as one market," he said.
His comments are echoed by brokers from the other Baltic states, who see a regional bourse as more eye-catching.
"A single bourse, one depository and one set of regulations would simplify things and draw in more money," said one Latvian broker.
But there are numerous hurdles which must be cleared first and few expect to see a pan-Baltic market for at least two or three years and possibly longer.
"It is obviously a very long-term project," said one Finnish-based broker active in the Baltics.
First regulations would have to be unified, and then a single-trading system would have to be adopted.

Estonia is the only Baltic market with continuous trade and price changes throughout the day. The bourses in Latvia and Lithuania have French-style, order driven systems with one price-fixing per session.
"The costs of meshing the systems will be quite high," says Andrejauskas.
The Baltic markets are also at different stages of development.
Estonia's, launched last year, is the youngest but the most liquid of the three.
Latvia's needs bigger, more profitable companies to really take off, analsyts say.
Lithuania is widely regarded as having the most potential in the long-term because it has a greater variety of sectors and companies as well as the largest population in the region.
But for the short-term at least, it is plauged by liquidity shortages and local investors have been fightened by a long, painful correction which set in after a January bull-run.
